title: The first sermon
hookLine: the middle way, the four truths, the eightfold path, at Isipatana (SN 56.11)

cards: First speeches often vanish. The opening lecture of a new science, the first talk of a movement: nobody wrote it down, nobody knew it would matter. Buddhist tradition says it kept this one.
Five men in a grove near Benares, and a man they once thought had given up is about to speak. They've agreed to listen. What he says is short, and monks still chant it.
It sets out a whole path in a few plain lists.

teach.h: DHAMMA, THE TEACHING. CAKKA, A WHEEL.
teach.b: Dhammacakka. Dhamma is the teaching, the way things are. Cakka is a wheel.

The first sermon is the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta: the teaching that set the wheel of the dhamma turning. Some readers hear in it the old Indian picture of a wheel-turning king, whose rule rolls out across the land.
Here the wheel isn't an army. It's an idea set in motion. He starts, of all places, with what to avoid.
Two extremes, he tells the five. One is chasing pleasure, living for the senses. The other is punishing yourself, starving, torturing the body.
These five know that second road well; they walked it with him. Neither works, he says. There is a middle way.

teach.h: FOUR TRUTHS, LIKE A DOCTOR'S VISIT.
teach.b: Then come the four noble truths. First: there is dukkha, the unsatisfactoriness in life: birth, aging, sickness, losing what you love, getting what you don't want.
Second: it has a cause, craving, the thirst that keeps reaching. Third: it can end. When the thirst is let go, the suffering it feeds goes too.
Fourth: there's a path to that end, in eight parts: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.
This isn't a creed about gods or a story about how the world began. Some readers hear it as a doctor's visit: the illness, the cause, the good news that it can heal, the treatment.
And the wheel turns up in surprising places. There's one in the middle of India's flag.
It comes from the time of Ashoka, an Indian emperor who supported the Buddhist community, and whose stone pillar stood at the Deer Park itself.

how: Monks and laypeople in Theravada communities chant the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, especially on Asalha Puja, the full-moon day that remembers the first sermon, and the dharma wheel appears on temples, flags and books.

games.why: he starts with two roads to avoid, pleasure-chasing and self-torture, and the middle way between. the five knew the second road well.

practice: Think of one thing that's bothering you this week, and walk it quietly through the four truths in your own words.
There's this ache; it comes from wanting something to be different; it could loosen; and here's one small step toward that. No need to fix anything, just see if the shape fits.

wordCard.voice: Dhammacakka. The wheel of the dhamma: the teaching set in motion at the Deer Park, with the middle way, four truths and an eightfold path.

orig.note: Pali: the wheel of the dhamma. The first sermon 'sets it turning' (pavattana).

carryVoice: Your line: the wheel turns. Five men in a grove heard it first. Sixty-two days in.
